utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Groome, we obtained from Mr. Domazet yesterday an agreement that because he was not in a position to call his experts, that the Prosecution case in reply could proceed and -- but he said he had not received any statements. Can you help us, what is going to happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure who made such an agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't know about an agreement. We received an agreement from Mr. Domazet. Your case in reply is due to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me first state for the record my recollection of the events of the last couple of weeks. The week before last, Mr. Domazet notified myself, and I believe the Chamber, that his case would be finishing early. I spoke with your legal officer and asked would you like us to try to have the case start as soon as possible after he finished, and I was told yes. Last week, Mr. Domazet notified us that he could not have Dr. Stojkovic until the 10th of December. At that point, I told the investigators to cease the attempts to get the two or three witnesses I thought I could produce this week and to move on to other important preparation for the rebuttal case. I believe yesterday is the first time now that the Prosecution was notified that the Court wishes to change the order of the trial as provided for in the Rules. Unfortunately, I am not prepared, just having returned myself last night, to produce witnesses today or I don't believe even for the remainder of this week. I can speak with the investigators and we can make every effort possible to try to accelerate the production of witnesses. Might I suggest that I think the best way that the Prosecution can expedite the conclusion of this trial is to focus this week on the psychiatric report which we just received yesterday, to begin to prepare rebuttal for that, and as well as some of the rebuttal witnesses, I will have to speak to and travel to see, some to convince to come and some because they've never been interviewed before. They are recently discovered. But may I suggest to the Court that perhaps the quickest way for the Prosecution to present a tightly-focused and short rebuttal case would be to prepare for it in advance of simply just working helter-skelter to bring witnesses to the Hague as soon as possible. As I said to the Court, the Prosecution rebuttal case will under no circumstances be longer than a week, and I am quite sure that it will be substantially less than a week, but I will make every effort to try to conclude the Prosecution rebuttal case as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But you still haven't answered my question, Mr. Groome, whether you were told yesterday or any other time that we expected you to start immediately. We would have expected you to have some statements. Now, have you no statements from any of these witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, one of the witnesses will be a witness that has already testified and Mr. Domazet already has the statements of that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And is the evidence to be given in reply to the Defence case in that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then what is the point of this? You know the rules: You want to call a witness, you give a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the majority of the Defence witnesses, I was provided absolutely no statement, perhaps half a sentence or at most two sentences regarding the -- what the Defence witnesses were going to testify to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I have already criticised Mr. Domazet almost continuously about his lack of preparation but that doesn't excuse the Prosecution, which has vastly greater resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure that the Prosecution has as much resources as the Court believes. If the Court wishes me to provide statements of all the witnesses, there are a number of newly discovered witnesses, they have never been interviewed by the Prosecution. That will obviously increase the amount of time if the Court is requiring the Prosecution to go out, interview them, take sworn statements and produce them prior to their testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Nobody said anything about a sworn statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Or any statement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then how is Mr. Domazet to be prepared to meet your case in reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will provide Mr. Domazet all the information that I have and any notes that I may take when I interview these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But why hasn't it been done already? If I may say so, Mr. Groome, and I have to say this, if we were able to have your services here, and I leave aside the problem of last week, but if we could have had your services full-time, I am sure that you would have done this. I cannot believe that anybody who is experienced in running a case, who knows they are going to get a right of reply on a number of issues which were raised for the first time in a case, that they would not be prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that you publicly criticised me yesterday and I would like to chance to read that transcript and respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I said that we did not have your full-time attention here because it is well known that you are involved in another case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm involved in two other cases and two of them are before you, Your Honour, and I think you've always known that I've been involved in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Groome, don't try to avoid the issue. I'm not talking about cases coming up for trial in this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, this Court has had my full attention. We have worked full days for most of the -- since the trial has started. The Prosecution brought its case or presented its case in less time than originally estimated to the Chamber. I think I've done everything possible to meet the Court's concerns about time in this matter. I apologise that I was not able to be here for the last two days but that was unavoidable. I've made every effort to handle this case as expeditiously as possible. I would -- and I would like the opportunity to go back and be able to state with more specificity the efforts that I've made in that regard, but I've done everything to try to expedite despite the Defence -- late notice on a number of items, to expedite copies of x-rays, to do all sorts of things to help expedite this case, despite the late notice that the Prosecution was given on a number of issues. I would take issue with the Court's criticism that the Court has not had my full efforts or full attention in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I've already said we understand the problems that arose for you personally at the end of last week and I criticise you not at all in relation to that. But the Milosevic case has taken, I am sure, more of your time than could possibly be warranted in a case like this where everybody knew that because of the log jam of cases which are about to start next year, we have not got the time to let this case run. Now, leaving aside everything that you have done, and we readily concede that you've got the Prosecution case through expeditiously, and we're very grateful for that, but nevertheless, with a constant stream of issues arising during the course of the Defence case, which arose because the Defence had not properly been prepared to cross-examine your witnesses and to raise the issues, I would have expected counsel to be ready to run a reply case. Now, you've got to be very careful about this. You keep on talking about newly-discovered witnesses. The evidence can only be given in reply to matters raised for the first time in the Defence case. You don't have a complete open slate to run any issue you like in a case in reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm well aware of the limitation of the case in reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I have some difficulty in seeing how you are going to get in the evidence of a number of apparently lay witnesses on issues which have been raised for the first time in the case -- in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would submit the greatest delay in this case is the psychiatric defence which was raised for the first time last week and I've yet to read the report. Even if I were able to put on all of the rebuttal witnesses starting today for the remainder of it, I would certainly need -- the Court would have to give me sufficient time to have my expert examine the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Nobody's expecting you to respond to a report that was given, at the earliest, last weekend. You are running a red herring there. Nobody would expect you to be able to meet that case. I'm talking about the factual issues. And there are a few factual issues which have arisen for the first time in the Defence case which were not put to your witnesses and which should be put to your witnesses. Those are the matters I would have expected you to be ready to run.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Court must also recognise that these witnesses are in a different country, it's not simply a matter of sending the investigator out to pick them up. I had them making preparations to have some of them available this week, but based on misrepresentations regarding Dr. Stojkovic and the Court's agreeing to allow him to extend or keep his case open until the 10th or the 11th of December, it seemed at that stage that it was impossible for the Prosecution to call any of its rebuttal witnesses before the new year, and that's why I told the investigators to prepare those witnesses for the 7th of January or the 9th of January, the first day back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This Tribunal recognises, for example, that an accused person should not be required to start his case until the Prosecution case is finished and that is because there are certain rights which arise at the end of the Prosecution case. But there is no such demarcation between the Defence case and the case in reply, and I have been in a number of cases where the Prosecution has started its case in reply because of problems the Defence has had. It maintains the right to reply to anything they may lead after the Prosecution case or the Prosecution witnesses have been called. If it arises during the case, they can bring those witnesses back. But we are under enormous pressure in this Tribunal to start six cases next year and that was planned upon the assumption that this case would be finished, and we simply do not have the courtrooms. We can't even go to Utrecht because that courtroom is being used for the appeal in the Lockerbie matter. So there is nowhere we can go and we've got to get this case finished and I -- nobody suggested that you could just sit back and wait for Dr. Stojkovic to come along.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, then I apologise for misunderstanding the Court's statements last week for the practice in the Tribunal of not adhering to the rules as far as the order of trial is concerned. I was unaware that it was the practice of the Tribunal to begin a rebuttal case in the middle of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then where are we going to go next?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, if the Court wishes, I will try to see if I can have those witnesses brought up. I would think the earliest I am going to be able to bring them up here is next Monday, the 10th. One of the remedies that the Court said that it would permit, based on the late psychiatric notice, was the re-opening of the defendant's cross-examination on the psychiatric evidence. I will read that report today and advise the Court whether I would be applying to reopen the cross-examination of him based on that report and I will make every effort to try to expedite the examination of the accused by our psychiatric expert, and some of the other issues that have arisen to the work with due diligence to get those matters completed as soon as possible so that the Prosecution is ready to present its rebuttal case as soon as we begin again in the new year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you served the report yet of your expert on the x-rays?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On the -- sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: On the x-rays.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I am scheduled to go and meet with that expert one day this week, and he has not completed his report but I will have that hopefully by the end of this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not criticising you about that because we still -- I have not yet seen the Defendant's one and it is an issue which has been running the whole of this year, so Mr. Domazet, with all due respect to him, should hang his head in shame in relation to the lateness of that report. But you've now got it so, if I may say so, that's a matter that you should pay some attention to because it is probably one of your biggest issues in the case, I should think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I recognise that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Well, let's see what Mr. Domazet's got to say about the progress of Dr. Stojkovic. What do you want to do with him? Are you going to seek to have a videolink?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as Dr. Stojkovic is concerned, he has informed me that he is simply unable to make himself available as a witness before mid-December, so I will try to have him available on the first working day in January. The other thing is I can forgo this witness. I don't see any other solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's on the 9th of January, you say you can have Dr. Stojkovic here. What about Dr. Jovicevic, what are you going to do about him?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. [Interpretation] I was not able to find Dr. Jovicevic. He's not in Uzice. I don't know exactly where he is at the moment. However, I will try in the following days to see whether I can secure his presence as well. In the meantime, I will provide the medical certificate concerning him, but I think that it would be very good if I am -- if I can manage to secure his presence as a witness as well, the thing we discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But is he able to travel to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what we discussed recently, no. If the operation goes well, he will be able to travel at the beginning of January. Otherwise, I would inform you in due time of the necessity to organise a videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When you say "due time," Mr. Domazet, as I understand it, they need three weeks' notice in order to organise this so it may be necessary to start that in train now because there's no way we can get a videolink before next Tuesday. So you better make up your mind about that one and start the train of actions that are required to get a videolink up also for the 9th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: In the meantime, you can produce the medical certificate as you wish. Well, now, Mr. Groome, does that mean we now do nothing until next Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I mean, the Prosecution has plenty of work to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Trial Chamber. We also have plenty of work to do but we're meant to be doing it in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I fully expected to have a Defence case to meet or to cross-examine the witnesses. I don't see how I can answer the question of what the Trial Chamber should do. I've already explained the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm asking when are we going to resume in court? I thought that was fairly clear but I'll say it directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will read the Defence psychiatric report this morning and, by noon, I will advise your legal officer whether I will be seeking to reopen the cross-examination of Mr. Vasiljevic. I would ask for the afternoon to prepare that cross-examination if I was going to reopen it. I will also, if the Court wishes, I will reopen the preparations to try to have the -- some of those rebuttal witnesses brought to The Hague and I will keep the Court posted regarding what the prospects are of having them here as soon as possible and advise the Court when that might be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you see Mr. Domazet's expectations about Dr. Stojkovic are becoming less and less hopeful. We're now talking about the middle of December, which is far too late for us because next Tuesday is our last sitting day and we are sitting on Tuesday. In case you were not here when I announced it, despite the Milosevic hearing, we have been granted permission by security to continue to use this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to clear up what the Court is perceiving as my divided attention, this is my primary attention. It's never been divided and it will not be. As long as this case is on trial, the Court will have me, it can be assured that I will never be taken away to work on any other case, including the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We're very grateful for that assurance but it has not been our perception, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would then ask the Court please to state with more particularity because I believe that I have given my full attention to this trial and would take issue with any -- or would like a chance to respond to any feeling that the Court might have regarding how my attention has not been fully directed towards this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I merely said that had been our perception. I'm not challenging what you have said. Our perception has certainly not been that you have had your full attention to this case because one does understand what has been going on in that other case and the time that has been devoted to it, and I am happy to accept your assurances that our perception was wrong, but I am just telling you that that has been our perception to date.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would like to respond to specific instances if the Court can make them aware to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I don't understand why you don't listen to what you are seeking to respond to. I said I am happy to accept your assurances that our perception was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you still persist in asking for specific details?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I guess not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, will you let us know if you are able to cross-examine the accused tomorrow? Then we'll certainly be here to do it. Thursday, unfortunately, as we have already said is not available. Friday is available and so are Monday and Tuesday. If you can bring any witnesses of factual issues along and give Mr. Domazet at least some sort of a summary of what they are going to give evidence on, by all means do so because I think that we have to get rid of whatever witnesses we can. The Prosecution's rights are fully protected. If anything happens in any of Mr. Domazet's still uncalled witnesses, then you have a right to reply to it, but I want to make it clear because sometimes I have a terrible feeling that the Office of the Prosecution has a different idea about what a case in reply is to what I understand it to be, but it must be limited to matters which have been raised by the Defence in the course of its case for the first time which it should have raised with your witnesses in the Prosecution case. Very well, then. Well, then we will now have to adjourn unless there's something more that anybody wants to raise. Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Trial Chamber I could have started a lot earlier than we thought to use this courtroom. I'm sorry that you've had this early start but it was, unfortunately, a muddle-up in the registry which led to it, which was compounded by further problems last night, and I'm grateful that everybody was able to get here, notwithstanding the short notice they were given by the registry. Very well, we will adjourn until further notice. -- Whereupon the hearing adjourned sine die at 9.25 a.m.
